newsitem.title: UK: Buba could lose $2.0 bln/yr in EMU shareout-report.
newsitem.headline: Buba could lose $2.0 bln/yr in EMU shareout-report.

text.p: Germany's Bundesbank risks losing $2.0 billion a year after European monetary union as the profits of the planned European System of Central Banks (ESCB) are shared out, a British financial journal said on Tuesday.
France, however, stands to gain up to $1.4 billion annually, while Britain -- if it joins EMU -- would benefit by $1.6 billion, said monetary policy quarterly Central Banking.
"Germany has such a large share of the monetary base and won't have such a large share of the shareholding of the EMI," said Neil Courtis, the author of the report.
The EMI (European Central Bank) is the forerunner to the European Central Bank (ECB).

The Maastricht Treaty calls for central profits to be divided by shareholdings in the ECB, according to the following formula -- 50 percent for share of EU population and 50 percent for share of EU GDP.

Central Banking's calculations showed Germany would have a 28 percent shareholding in a 12-member ECB, while its monetary base -- cash in circulation plus credit institutions' deposits with the central bank -- would total around $202 billion, or 41.95 percent of the European monetary base.

France has a monetary base of over $56 billion, or 11.7 percent of the European total, with an ECB shareholding of 21 percent. Britain's shareholding is 19 percent, but its $41 billion monetary base represents just 8.5 percent of the total, the report said.
Sweden, the Netherlands, Austria and Spain would lose out, while the redistribution would benefit Portugal, Belgium, Finland and Luxembourg and prove neutral for Ireland.
Most of a central bank's profits come from "seignorage," a term describing the money they make from printing banknotes.

According to the Maastricht Treaty, the seignorage revenue, or monetary income, of central banks locked into the single currency will be pooled and redistributed according to their shareholdings in the European Central Bank, the report said.

Until Europe's central banks standardise their balance sheets, a bank's monetary income and thus its contribution to the pool will be calculated by adding up its monetary base and applying to it a "pre-determined rate of income," Courtis wrote.
Though the EMI had not yet finalised the methodology for calculating the rate, a modest 3.1 percent rate would be a conveniently low assumption, he said.
Even at such a modest rate, Germany would lose more than $2.0 billion a year.
"The problem for Germany is stark: in a European Central Bank of 12 (members), they will have 42 percent of the monetary base, but only a 28 percent shareholding," said Courtis.
"No matter how the technicians try to refine their models, the Bundesbank must eventually lose out."
